structure.title: Returning soldiers and courtships
structure.text: The household welcomes visitors, establishing two romances with very different styles of speaking.

structure.title: Arranged belief
structure.text: Staged conversations and misleading appearances test how readily people accept evidence about those they desire.

people.name: Beatrice and Benedick
people.text: A sharp-tongued lady and a soldier who has sworn never to marry, who can't stop sparring whenever they meet.

people.name: Hero and Claudio
people.text: The governor's gentle daughter and a young officer who fall in love almost at first sight, and whose wedding is quickly arranged.

people.name: Don John
people.text: The prince's resentful illegitimate brother, recently defeated and reconciled, who is looking for a way to make mischief.

context.title: Reputation and gender
context.text: Accusations about sexual conduct carry unequal consequences. A woman's public standing can depend on other people's willingness to hear her.

context.title: Overhearing
context.text: Hearing something supposedly not intended for one's ears can make it seem especially credible. The play repeatedly exploits that assumption.

notice.why: Verbal friction can conceal attention that easy agreement lacks.
Social prestige and competence do not reliably coincide.

opening: Beatrice and Benedick enjoy insulting each other so much that their friends suspect a little encouragement could turn the habit into love. Nearby, a younger couple needs almost no encouragement at all. Shakespeare lets overheard conversations and staged evidence work on both romances, producing delight in one place and serious injury in another. The pleasure of watching clever people fooled sits beside a harsher discovery: a woman's reputation can be destroyed very quickly when a man finds suspicion easier than asking her what happened.
